body:
Inflammation and lipid accumulation are hallmark features of atherosclerosis, a leading cause of death and morbidity worldwide. Our previous study identified PARP9 (protein mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase) and PARP14, enzymes that catalyze ADP-ribosylation of proteins, as molecular switches of proinflammatory versus anti-inflammatory macrophage function, yet direct evidence of ADP-ribosylation was lacking.
1
These findings incited the current study, which is the unveiling of the ADP-ribosylome of atherosclerosis and fatty liver, illuminating a crucial aspect of the disease’s molecular landscape. All animal procedures were performed in compliance with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol no. 003-2020). Low-density lipoprotein receptor–deficient (
Ldlr
−/−
) mice were fed a regular chow or a high-fat diet (HFD) for 3 or 6 months before harvesting the aorta and liver (Figure [A]). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated increased ADP-ribosyl signal in lipid-rich and macrophage-rich aortic lesions of HFD-fed
Ldlr
−/
−
mice as compared with chow diet controls (Figure [B]).
See accompanying editorial on page
2140
Figure.
Profiling the ADP-ribosylome of
Ldlr
−/− mice. A
, Study workflow. Experimental design to characterize the ADP-ribosylome in the aorta, liver, and plasma of male mice fed a chow (catalog no. 5008i; LabDiet) or high-fat diet (HFD; Clinton/Cybulsky High-Fat Rodent Diet, 1.25% cholesterol, catalog no. D12108Ci; Research Diets Inc) for 3 or 6 months. Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 equipped with RiboMaP (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for mass spectral processing. The resulting ADP-ribosyl peptides and proteins for the aorta and liver are summarized.
B
, Immunohistochemistry. Representative 6-month aortic Oil Red O (ORO; catalog no. 26079-15; Citifluor-EMS), ADP-ribosylation (catalog no. 83732; Cell Signaling Technology), and macrophage (CD68 staining, catalog no. 53444; Abcam) staining and quantification of the 3- and 6-month chow or HFD groups. n=7 mice per group. Scale bar=100 µm.
C
, ADP-ribosylation profiling in aorta. Volcano plots show differentially abundant ADP-ribosyl peptides with featured peptides, their identity scores (XCorr, p-series score), and false discovery rate (FDR) threshold. Representative images of aorta underscore extent of fatty tissue by 6 months; representative APO A
1
spectra from liver and aorta.
D
, ADP-ribosylation profiling in liver vs aorta. Volcano plots showing differentially abundant ADP-ribosyl peptides, and Venn diagrams depicting the extent of overlapping proteins between liver and aorta.
E
, ADP-ribosylation signatures in plasma using Western blotting and mass spectrometry. Anti–ADP-ribosylation analysis of lipoprotein fractions isolated from wild-type (WT; 3 months old) and
Ldlr
−/−
mice fed a chow or HFD for 6 months. Chylomicron (CM), VLDL (very-low density lipoprotein), LDL (low-density lipoprotein), HDL (high-density lipoprotein). Annotated bands were confirmed with mass spectrometry. Mass spectrometric analysis identified 3 ADP-ribosylated proteins in WT plasma, including APO A
1
and ALB (spectra are shown), supporting their likely secretion from the liver.
F
, Immunohistochemistry of human plaques. Colocalization of ADP-ribosylation (catalog no. 83732; Cell Signaling Technology) and macrophages (CD68 staining, catalog no. ab213363; Abcam) in human carotid plaques. These images represent carotid endarterectomy specimens from 3 different patients (Brigham and Women’s Hospital Institutional Review Board protocol no. 1999P001348, PI: Peter Libby) that exhibited similar results. Scale bar=100 µm. For additional information, please see the Major Resources Table in the
Supplemental Material
. Statistics: Immunohistochemistry (
B
)—Mann-Whitney
U
test tests were performed (HFD vs chow diet, at each time point), using Prism (version 10.4.0, GraphPad Software, CA). Proteomics (
C
and
D
). For each tissue and time point proteome, we performed a 2-group differential analysis (HFD vs chow diet) using median-normalized and log-transformed protein group intensities. Differential abundance was assessed using the Limma package, which applies an empirical Bayes moderated
t
test. False discovery rates (
q
values) were computed using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Aorta plots represent the mean of 4 replicates per group (diet and month), where each replicate is a pool of 10 whole aortas; liver plots represent the mean of 6 replicates per group, where each replicate is a single liver. ADPr indicates ADP-ribosylation; AOI, area of interest; CD, cluster of differentiation; C-term, C-terminus; H2BC3, histone H2B type 1-B; H3-3A, histone H3.3; and N-term, N-terminus.
Ten aortas were pooled to acquire the minimum 10 mg protein required for ADP-ribosylomics (n=4 pools per mouse group); whereas 6 individual livers were sufficient to achieve this yield (Figure [A]). Our recently established ion mobility mass spectrometry strategy enabled us to discover the ADP-ribosylome signatures of experimental atherosclerosis and fatty liver.
2
Mass spectra were processed with SEQUEST-HT (Proteome Discoverer v2.5; Thermo). ADP-ribosylome-unique parameters included the ADP-ribosyl modification, the p-series score from RiboMaP, our spectral annotation tool specifically for ADP-ribosyl peptides,
3
and the export of ADP-ribosyl peptides to represent the ADP-ribosylome. Of note, we previously established that a 5% false discovery rate is appropriate for ADP-ribosyl peptides, provided the spectra are also scored for the p-series ions using RiboMaP.
3
From the combined diets and time points, we detected 1758 ADP-ribosyl peptides (1% false discovery rate) corresponding to 575 ADP-ribosylated liver proteins and 170 ADP-ribosyl peptides (5% false discovery rate) corresponding to 126 ADP-ribosylated aortic proteins (Figure [A]). Focusing on the changes to the aorta (Figure [C], volcano plots), we feature ADP-ribosyl APO A
1
, APO A
2
, APOE, and ALB (albumin) peptides (Figure [C]). At 3 months, most of these peptides increased with HFD (
P
≤0.002;
q
≤0.028) but were not detected or did not change at 6 months (Figure [C]). This latter observation is not surprising because solubilization of the 6-month aortas was challenging, owing to their high-fat content (Figure [C], gross images). We anticipated that apolipoproteins would be lost with the insoluble fat deposits. On the contrary, an ADP-ribosyl PARP9 peptide appeared at 6 months, with a higher abundance in HFD (
P
=0.049;
q
=0.246), and an ADP-ribosylated PARP14 shifted to a slight increase in HFD from 3 to 6 months (Figure [C]). These findings are consistent with PARP9’s and PARP14’s association with proinflammatory macrophages.
1
Our data indicate that ADP-ribosylated apolipoproteins identified in the aorta were secreted by the liver. We confirmed an increase in ADP-ribosylated apolipoproteins in the livers of HFD mice (Figure [D], volcano plots). ADP-ribosylated APO A
1
, APO A
2
, APOE, and ALB, as well as HBB-BS (hemoglobin subunit beta like 1), 2 histones, and ITGB2 (integrin beta-2), increased in HFD in both tissues (Figure [D], venn diagram). Our previous study established that systemic IFN-y (interferon gamma) induced changes to the ADP-ribosylation of lipid-binding proteins in the liver of wild-type mice.
3
Although we did not detect any differences in their modification statuses, we also identified ADP-ribosylated APO A
1
and APO A
2
,
3
indicating that the liver of wild-type mice also secretes ADP-ribosylated apolipoproteins.
3
Anti–ADP-ribosylation Western blotting (pool of 6 mice, 10 μg protein analyzed) confirmed signal in lipoprotein and lipid-poor fractions of both wild-type and
Ldlr
−/−
plasma with ADP-ribosylation signal intensity (Western blot) coinciding with protein intensity (Coomassie blue; Figure [E]). However, our previous work also demonstrated that Western blotting does not necessarily reflect the complex changes to ADP-ribosylation.
3
Nonetheless, ADP-ribosylomics of plasma remains a frontier, notably of lipid-laden plasma. For instance, 5 mL of pooled wild-type mice plasma recovered only 3 ADP-ribosylated proteins—APO A
1
, ALB, and HBA-A1 (hemoglobin subunit alpha; Figure [E]). Despite the low yield, these preliminary findings support that the apolipoproteins circulate in this modified form (Figure [E]).
Most ADP-ribosyl peptides mapped to the C terminus of APO A
1
(Figure [E]), which initiates lipids and cholesterol solubilization. Relative to other modifications, such as glycation, ADP-ribosylation is larger and can form polymers up to 200 units long. Because glycation reduces APO A
1
stability and cholesterol-efflux capability,
4
ADP-ribosylation may have similar effects. Our long-term efforts include innovations to profile deeper into the plasma ADP-ribosylome and to conduct meaningful functional studies. For instance, site-directed mutagenesis of ADP-ribosylated acceptor sites could impact other modifications, namely methyl groups that have been described on the equivalent lysines in the human APO A
1
homolog.
5
Although gain-of-ADP-ribosylation studies are more feasible, differing PARP activity in vitro and in vivo requires careful design and interpretation. Nonetheless, assays that exploit the established lipid and cholesterol-binding properties of APO A
1
will streamline our efforts.
This unbiased proteomics study demonstrated that atherosclerotic lesions of
Ldlr
−/−
mice accumulate ADP-ribosylated proteins. We also revealed that ADP-ribosylation associates with macrophage-rich areas in human plaques (Figure [F]). Our discoveries provide novel molecular bases for the development of more effective future therapeutics and biomarkers for inflammatory vascular disease.
